title: Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage, Conclusion
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Here is a summary of the talk in 4-6 sentences: Joden Bob Rose invites the audience to cultivate mindfulness and inner peace through a simple yet profound practice: embracing simplicity and non-attachment by living in harmony with nature, as described in the "Song of the Grass Root Hermitage". This poem encourages us to let go of attachments and conditioning, and instead approach life with ease and vulnerability. By doing so, we can find freedom from worldly desires and delusions, and discover a sense of peace and stability that is always available, even in difficult times. Joden hopes to inspire the audience to reflect on the value of simplicity and non-attachment, and to incorporate this practice into their daily lives. Through this practice, we can quiet our minds and find our true nature, free from distractions and conditioning.
topics: Song of the Grass Root Hermitage

sentences.text: Ben Connolly will join us to lead the chant of the song of the grass root hut.
Take it away.

Hello, my name is Ben Connolly and I'm making this video because a few people have requested that I demonstrate how we chant the song of the grass root hermitage by Shito here at Minnesota Zen Meditation Center.
Chanting this poem, or really any poem you find inspiring, is a great way to take something that you value into your own voice and your own body.
So I think it is a really wonderful practice, and I encourage you to try it out or take it up as a regular part of your life.
We chant in a very simple style here.
We just chant a single pitch, and generally men and women chant one octave apart, with men chanting a very low note and women chanting a note that seems kind of low for them.

So if the men are chanting at a pitch like "song of the grass root hermitage," we'll be chanting one octave higher, "song of the grass root hermitage," which sounds pretty high when I chant it but in a woman's voice doesn't feel quite so high.
So anyway, I encourage you to take this practice up, and I will demonstrate the chant, song of the grass root hermitage.
*I built a grass hut where there's nothing of value.
After eating I relax and enjoy a nap.
When it was completed fresh weeds appeared.
Now it's been lived in, covered by weeds.
The person in the hut lives here calmly, not stuck to inside, outside or in between.
Places worldly people live he doesn't live.
Realms worldly people love he doesn't love.
Though the hut is small it includes the entire world.
In 10 feet square an old man illumines forms in their nature.
A great vehicle bodhisattva trusts without doubt.
The middling or lowly can't help wondering: will this hut perish or not?
Perishable or not, the original master is present.
Not dwelling south or north, east or west.
Firmly based on steadiness it can't be surpassed.
A shining window below the green pines.*
*Jade palaces or vermilion towers can't compare with it.
Just sitting with head covered, all things are at rest.
Thus this mountain monk doesn't understand at all.
Living here he no longer works to get free.
Who would proudly arrange seats trying to entice guests?
Turn around the light to shine within, then just return.
The vast inconceivable source can't be faced or turned away from.
Meet the ancestral teachers, be familiar with their instruction.
Find grasses to build a hut and don't give up.
Let go of hundreds of years and relax completely.
Open your hands and walk innocent.
Thousands of words, myriad interpretations, are only to free you from obstructions.
If you want to know the undying person in the hut, don't separate from this skin bag here and now.*
*May all the benefit of this recitation be dedicated to the well-being of everyone throughout space and time.*
Well, thank you for spending some time with me, and may you be happy and at peace.
Thank you all for bearing with the tech beginning.
Thanks Tammy.
Good evening friends.
Here we are for our final class on the song of the Grassroot Hermitage.
It seems like we just started, and it seems like we could start all over again and just keep digging and scratching and enjoying what we find.
Tonight we're going to do things a little bit differently.
I have a few introductory remarks, and then we sent out a question for you to consider, to think about, and it's going to be more of an open floor discussion, round table.
We won't go into breakout rooms, and we'll finish with my reading of the song of the Grassroot Hermitage to finish our session tonight.
So when we began we were considering this monk who had retreated to a ledge of stone as a hermit.
Tonight what I'd like to do is reflect on that hermit tradition with some passages.
Many of you know the work of Red Pine in his translations of the platform sutra, the heart sutra, and his great commentary.
Back in the early 90s Red Pine went to China on one of his many trips there, guided trips, and came back and wrote this book called Road to Heaven, Encounters with Chinese Hermits.
He went to China, and there are some wonderful, wonderful photographs by Steve Johnson in this book as well.
It's kind of a travel book, but it's also deeply embedded in scholarship and his knowledge of Chinese history and Buddhism.
He had this intuition, living in Taiwan where he lived in a monastery for a number of years, that there were still hermits in China, and by gosh he found a number of them.
They were still there sitting, some of them, for many many years in their caves and huts in the mountains.

So what I'd like to do tonight is to just give you a few excerpts from this book: both his sense of hermits and what they are like and how and why they lived, and a few passages that some of the wiser, in some cases, abbots of the various temples provided about their perspective on Zen.
I tried to pick passages that had resonance with the readings we've done in Song of the Grass Hut.
So Bill Porter of Red Pine begins saying:
*Stories about hermits in the hills of ancient China were my favorite stories.
I could understand someone wanting nothing more than to live a simpler life inside a cloud, under a pine tree, somewhere out of town, surviving on moonlight, taro, and hemp.
Other than a mountain, they didn't need much.
A little mud, some thatch, a patch of melons, a row of tea bushes, a trellis of chrysanthemums, and a break in the weather.
Since the Yellow Emperor's time, there must have been a million hermits in China, but reading about them made me wonder if they could have survived the 20th century.
I couldn't think of any great master who had achieved his understanding of the Dharma without first undergoing a period of seclusion.
In China, hermits have remained the most esteemed persons because hermits are sages.
They can see that to which others are blind and hear that to which others are deaf.*

Red Pine presents a little poem from the Han dynasty by a group known as the Four Worthies, four friends who instead of working in the court, which was the typical route of an educated person in China, to be a bureaucrat essentially, chose otherwise.
This poem was written around 200 BC, and we can hear resonances with the song of the Grass Hut.
*Forested mountains, winding valleys, bright purple mushrooms to keep away hunger.
With sages so distant, where can we turn?
Horses and carriages bring nothing but worries.
Merchants and kings are no match for paupers.*

*Whether or not they came out of retirement to serve, hermits have influenced the entire culture as springs of pure thinking and pure living that,* and this is the important point, *sooner or later find their way to town.
Dao Yuanming in one of his drinking poems provides a glimpse of the spirit that liberated China's followers of the Dao and that kept their minds, if not their bodies, free from city dust.*
*I built my hut beside a path, but here no cart or horse.
You ask how this can be.
A distant mind is a far-off place.
Picking mums by the eastern fence, I lose myself in the southern hills.
The mountain air, the sunset light, birds flying home together.
In this there is a truth to know but not to say.*
Red Pine and Steve Johnson visited a number of monasteries and abbots, and one abbot they visited at a monastery called Lukotani said this: *Man's nature is the same as the nature of heaven.
Heaven gives birth to all creatures and they all go in different directions, but sooner or later they return to the same place.
The goal of this universe, its highest goal, is nothingness.
Nothingness means return.
This is the body of the Dao.
Not only man but plants and animals and all living things are part of this body, are made of this body, this body of nothingness.
Everything is one with nothingness.
There aren't two things in this universe to realize.
This is the goal, not only of Daoism but also of Buddhism.
Everything in the world changes.
Daoists and Buddhists seek that which doesn't change.
This is why they don't seek fame or fortune.
They seek only the Dao, which is the nothingness of which we are all created and to which we all return.
Our goal is to be one with this natural process.*
Then he goes on to say: *The important thing is to live an upright life.
You don't have to be a monk or nun to do this.
It doesn't do any good to be a monk or nun if you don't keep the precepts.
What's important is to keep the precepts.
But anyone who leads an upright life does this.
This is the basis of practice.
The precepts are the demands you place on yourself.
Precepts make practice possible.
If you don't make demands on yourself, you won't get anywhere in your practice.*
*Regarding hermit monks and eating, after a meal I relax and take a nap.
Sometimes they eat once a day.
Sometimes once every three days.
Sometimes once a week.
As long as they are able to nourish their inner energy, they're fine and they don't need food.
They might meditate for one day, two days, a week, even several weeks.
You might have to wait a long time before they come out again.*
*Master Xue said the Tao isn't something that can be put into words.
You have to practice before you can understand.
Lao Tzu teaches us to be natural.
You can't force things, including practice.
Understanding is something that happens naturally.
It is different for everyone.
The main thing is to reduce your desires and quiet your mind.
Practice takes a long time and you have to stay healthy.
If you have a lot of thoughts and desires, you won't live long enough to reach the end.*
And Xu Tong, the abbot of Xianxi temple near Xian, had this to say: *In Zen, we keep asking, who's chanting the name of the Buddha?
All we think about is where the name of the Buddha is coming from.
We keep asking until we find out who we were before we were born.
This is when we sit with one mind, and if the mind runs off somewhere, we follow it wherever it goes until the mind finally becomes quiet.
Until there's no Zen to Zen, no question to question, until we reach the stage where we question without questioning, and without questioning, we keep questioning.
We keep questioning until we finally find an answer, until delusions come to an end, until we can swallow the world, all these rivers and mountains, everything, but the world can't swallow us.
Until we can ride the tiger, but the tiger can't ride us, until we find out who we really are.
This is Zen.*
He spent quite a bit of time with a female hermit named Yu Un Chao, who wrote him a letter, a note, that said this: *The essence of Buddhist practice: goodwill, compassion, joy, detachment.*
And the last personage I'll quote from Red Pine's journey is Chi Ching, who is the abbot of Xing Qing Temple, about continuing practice: *If people are quiet, they can be quiet anywhere.
If people aren't quiet, they won't be quiet here.
Everything depends on you.
Life is transient like a flash of lightning or a dream.
Eighty years pass like a cloud.
We are born and then we die.
But before we received this form, we had another face, our original face.
We can't see it with our eyes.
We can only know it with our wisdom.
The sutras say that which is beyond form is the Buddha.
We all have the Buddha nature.
We're all destined to become Buddhas.
But Buddhahood isn't something that can be achieved in a couple of days.
You have to practice before you can become aware of your original nature, your original face.*
Toward the end of the book, Red Pine says the recurring theme of China's hermit tradition is that it doesn't represent a renunciation of society so much as a renunciation of greed.
As a rule, hermits sought to reform society by first reforming themselves.
And many of them came, in this case, to the Taipaishan Mountains to cool their passions as hermits.

The final line in this book, and one that reflects both on the song of the grass hut and the reality of our practice as living in the 21st century where we are, is quite a well-known Chinese saying: *The small hermit lives on a mountain.
The great hermit lives in a town.*
So here we all are living in a town, in a town somewhere in the universe.
Some of us are in Vancouver.
Some of us are in Bellingham.
Some of us are many other places.
We have spent the last seven weeks reading the song of the grass-roof hermitage and had various breakout sessions, and I've tried to present some estimations and some parallel texts and ideas.
So we thought tonight it would be really appropriate to finish up our investigation.
Hopefully you continue your investigation on your own terms and your own time.
But tonight we'd like to hear what lines, what thoughts, what words resonated with you and have encouraged your practice, encouraged you to think about your practice differently.
Or maybe changed the way you look at life in a way that was totally unexpected because of engaging with this text, being eyebrows to eyebrows with Shitou for the last seven weeks.
